name: Battle of Uhud
info: The Quraysh of Mecca under Abu Sufyan ibn Harb fought the early Muslims under Muhammad near Mount Uhud, north of Medina, in March 625; the Muslims lost heavily after part of their archer force left its hill, and the Meccans withdrew without pressing on.

facts.place: A valley north of Medina near Mount Uhud, in present-day Saudi Arabia
facts.sides: The Quraysh of Mecca under Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, with a force of approximately 3,000 men, 700 of them in chain mail; the early Muslims under Muhammad, 1,000 men at first and around 700 after 300 withdrew, of whom 100 had chain mail
facts.outcome: The Muslims suffered heavy losses, among them Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and the Meccans withdrew without pressing home their advantage; scholars differ on whether this was a Muslim defeat or an indecisive result.

t: Muhammad posted 50 archers on a hill to guard the Muslim rear against the Meccan cavalry; when most of them went down to join the advance, Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry attacked the flank and rear.
Ibn al-Athir names 85 Muslims killed, 75 of them Medinans and 10 Emigrants from Mecca.
Chase F. Robinson calls the Muslim defeat clear enough, while William Montgomery Watt notes that the Meccans failed to achieve their aim of destroying Muhammad and his followers.
dyk: Abu Sufyan shouted from the mountain that victory in war goes by turns and that this day was in exchange for the day of Badr, and Umar ibn al-Khattab answered him by Muhammad's instruction.
ev: The Quraysh are defeated at Badr and several of their leaders are killed, among them Amr ibn Hisham
Abu Sufyan mobilises a force of over 3,000 men to retaliate for the losses at Badr
Muhammad yields to those who want to fight in the open, and the Muslims take position on the slopes of Uhud; Abd Allah ibn Ubayy withdraws with 300 men
Duels between standard-bearers open the fighting and the Meccan lines are pushed back
Most of the archers leave the hill, and Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry attacks the Muslim flank and rear; Hamza is killed
Umar leads a counter-charge that dislodges Khalid's forces from the slopes, and the fighting ceases
The Meccans halt at Hamra al-Asad, and Muhammad sends out a small force to scout them
Abu Sufyan and allied tribes attack Medina in the Battle of the Trench

sections.background:
After the Muslim emigration to Medina, hostilities with the Quraysh of Mecca grew, largely because of Muslim raids on Meccan trade caravans. Francis Peters proposes that the raids were a quick remedy for the poverty of Muhammad's people in their new land, who lacked agricultural skills and capital for trade. Tariq Ramadan agrees, and adds that the Battle of Badr in particular was meant to impress the Meccans, who were growing more hostile towards Medina.

Muhammad learned of a large Quraysh caravan, 1,000 camels laden with 50,000 dinars, travelling from Gaza to Mecca, and ordered his followers to ambush it. Abu Sufyan, who led the caravan, got wind of the plan and sent for help from Mecca while the caravan took another route. At Badr the Muslims defeated the larger Meccan force. A number of influential and experienced Quraysh men were killed, including Amr ibn Hisham, and their prestige was shaken. Old tribal enemies such as the Hawazin began to look to them again. Muhammad used the victory as proof of his prophethood, and those who joined his raids grew more numerous.

Abu Sufyan, chosen as successor to the leader of the Quraysh, vowed vengeance. Some months after Badr he went to Medina with 200 men, burned two houses and laid waste to some fields to fulfil his vow, and left. A few months later he mobilised an invasion force of over 3,000 men.
sections.forces:
Abu Sufyan ibn Harb led about 3,000 men towards Medina, 700 of them equipped with chain mail. According to the early Muslim historian Ibn Ishaq, several Meccan women accompanied the army to raise morale, among them Abu Sufyan's wife Hind bint Utba. The Meccans camped on the pastures north of the city, hoping to draw the Muslims into open battle. On the field Abu Sufyan held the centre, Ikrima, son of Amr ibn Hisham, the left flank and Khalid ibn al-Walid the right, while Amr ibn al-As commanded the cavalry and coordinated the attack of its two wings.

Muhammad had originally meant to stay in Medina and fight from its fortifications, aware that the Quraysh would struggle with a siege. Many Muslims who had missed Badr begged for an open battle, and he gave way and put on his armour. Three Muslim contingents totalling 1,000 men were assembled. Muhammad screened them in person and sent away those he judged too young, among them Abd Allah, son of Umar ibn al-Khattab. Only 100 men had chain mail. Shortly before the fighting Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, chief of the Khazraj, withdrew with 300 men and returned to Medina, reportedly because he disliked the plan to march out; the Qur'an later censures him and his followers for it.

The remaining force, around 700, took position on the lower slopes of Uhud with the mountain at its back. Muhammad placed 50 archers on a rocky hill on the west side of the camp, to keep the Meccan cavalry, which outnumbered the Muslim horse fifty to one, from circling round the army.
sections.course:
Muhammad told the archers to keep their place whether the battle went for or against the army, so that the Muslims could not be attacked from their direction. The Meccan charge, led by the Medinan exile Abu Amir, was driven back by a shower of stones. The Meccan standard-bearer Talha ibn Abi Talha al-Abdari then challenged the enemy to a duel, and Ali ibn Abi Talib struck him down. Talha's brother Uthman took up the fallen banner and Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib killed him. Talha's brothers and sons came forward one by one until they had all perished. A general engagement followed, and the Muslims swept through the Meccan ranks.

The Meccan cavalry's repeated attempts on the left Muslim flank were beaten off by the archers, and the Muslims pierced the Meccan lines with victory seeming certain. Most of the archers then ran downhill to join the advance and plunder the Meccan camp, which disobeyed Muhammad's orders to stay put. Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry attacked the few archers who held their place and then overran the Muslim flank and rear. In the confusion many Muslims were killed, Hamza among them, struck down by a javelin thrown by Wahshi ibn Harb. A rumour spread that Muhammad had been killed; he had been wounded in the face by stones.

Many Muslims fled and regrouped higher up the slopes. Umar ibn al-Khattab rallied them at the foot of the mountain and, on Muhammad's instruction to keep the Meccans from the high ground, led a counter-charge that dislodged Khalid's men. The cavalry could not climb the slopes, and the fighting ceased.
sections.aftermath:
Before leaving, Abu Sufyan went up the mountain and called out that victory in war goes by turns and that the day was in exchange for Badr. By Ibn Ishaq's account Umar answered at Muhammad's bidding that the two sides were not equal, since their dead were in paradise and the Meccans' in hell. Abu Sufyan asked whether Muhammad was dead, and Umar replied that he could hear every word. Abu Sufyan then returned to Mecca without attacking the wounded Muslims again.

Ibn al-Athir names 85 Muslims killed, 75 of them Medinans (43 from the Banu Khazraj and 32 from the Banu Aws) and 10 Emigrants from Mecca; 46 of the 85 had fought at Badr. The hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari puts the dead at seventy. Hind bint Utba and her companions are said to have mutilated the Muslim dead, and Hind is reported to have cut open Hamza's body and tried to eat his liver. The Muslims buried their dead on the field and went home that evening.

The Meccans halted that night at Hamra al-Asad, a few miles from Medina. Next morning Muhammad sent a small force to scout them; according to Watt he judged that a show of force was needed to speed them away. The Meccans, unwilling to look chased off, stayed nearby for a few days. Al-Waqidi has Amr ibn al-As say that the Meccans left because they had many wounded and all their horses had been wounded by arrows, and because they feared that Ibn Ubayy and others who had held back might attack them.
sections.sources:
Most of what is known comes from the sira and maghazi traditions, the biographical narratives and campaign accounts of the early Muslim centuries. Ibn Ishaq's biography of Muhammad gives the main narrative, and the general sequence of events gained consensus early. Accounts of the battle derive mainly from descendants of the participants. Al-Waqidi and al-Ya'qubi also give accounts, and they differ on who stayed beside Muhammad in the crisis: al-Ya'qubi names Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zubayr ibn al-Awwam and Talha ibn Ubayd Allah, al-Waqidi fourteen companions, seven Emigrants and seven Ansar, and he records another account in which eight companions swore to fight to the death.

The Qur'an refers to the battle in verses such as 3:122, 3:152 and 3:166 to 168, and Safi al-Rahman al-Mubarakpuri connects 8:36 with it; Ibn Kathir's commentary on that verse, citing Ibn Ishaq, ties it to the wealth Quraysh men spent to fight Muhammad. Sahih al-Bukhari preserves hadith on the archers under Abd Allah ibn Jubayr (3039) and on those who turned back (1884). All of these are Islamic sources, and the Meccan side is known only through them.

Chase F. Robinson judges the basic narrative and chronology reasonably authentic, but finds some of the more elaborate details, such as the exact scale of the Muslim defeat, doubtful or hard to establish. Historians also disagree on the outcome: Robinson holds that a disheartening Muslim defeat is clear enough, while Watt notes that the Meccans failed in their strategic aim and that their withdrawal suggests weakness.
sections.legacy:
The battle is seen as a significant setback for the Muslims and a minor victory for the Quraysh, who returned with an even larger force in the Battle of the Trench in 627. Abu Sufyan, whose leadership was no longer disputed, began building alliances with nomadic tribes. Two Muslim parties were killed in ambushes, among them instructors led into a trap by guides of a tribe that had asked for them. Muhammad then became convinced that the Banu Nadir were plotting against him, and after a fifteen-day siege they were expelled from Medina.

For the Muslims the battle had a religious as well as a military side. They had expected another victory like Badr, which they took as a sign of God's favour. A verse of the Qur'an revealed soon after, 3:152, names disobedience and desire for loot as the cause of the setback, and the tradition reads the losses as partly a punishment and partly a test of steadfastness. Firestone observes that such verses gave the Muslims inspiration and hope and made their later battles sacred, and that the battle seemed to strengthen their solidarity rather than demoralise them. It is also noted for the emergence of Khalid ibn al-Walid, who later became one of the best known Arab generals in the conquests of the Sassanid Empire and of Byzantine Syria.

A modern military assessment praises Muhammad's choice of ground. The front was about 730 to 820 metres wide, with Mount Einein on one flank and the defiles of Uhud on the other, so that only the approach guarded by the archers lay open to the Meccan cavalry. The cave on Mount Uhud where Muhammad rested has drawn attention since some Salafi scholars proposed destroying it; local authorities rejected the calls and moved to protect the site.

summary: At Uhud in March 625 the Meccans under Abu Sufyan fought the Muslims of Medina under Muhammad. The Muslims were winning until most of their archers left the hill and Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry struck the rear. Scholars differ on whether it was a defeat or an indecisive result.

notes: The article dates the battle to Saturday 23 March 625 (7 Shawwal, 3 AH) but also says the Muslim army set out late on Friday, 21 December 624: the two cannot both be right. I used the first and left out the second.

The Muslim force: 1,000 at the start, 'around 700' after Ibn Ubayy's 300 left. The article does not say whether the 100 with chain mail are of the 1,000 or the 700; I wrote 'of whom 100 had chain mail' loosely in facts, consider trimming.

Meccan losses: none given in the article; I say so in the aftermath (a plain statement of absence in the article, left because the editor should know). Consider cutting that sentence if the page should not note it.
The article's bare statement that the Meccan cavalry outnumbered the Muslim cavalry 'with 50-to-1' is its own figure; given without an attribution.
The 'Importance in warfare' assessment is unattributed in the article; I called it 'a modern military assessment'.

The article's 'The very cautious Abu Sufyan' and 'The Holy Prophet' wording was not carried over. The mutilation reports are kept as 'said to' and 'reported'. The Quranic and hadith blocks are used only for what the texts record.
The article names Ibn Ubayy's withdrawal and says he was later censured in the Qur'an; kept as 'the Qur'an later censures'. The 'hell' and 'paradise' answer is attributed to Ibn Ishaq's account.
Left out: the long Qur'an and Ibn Kathir quotations, Bukhari's 'twelve men remained' detail, the list of notable dead beyond Hamza, the Hubal call, Ibn Qami'a's claim.
